title: What Your Questions Are Actually Saying
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli (with guest co-author Elina) argues that a manager's questions do far more than gather information: they set the psychological weather of a conversation and signal whether competence is assumed or doubted. She treats bad questions as a design problem rather than a moral one, and breaks a question into three facets, intent, design and signal. She then names four families that predictably create friction (assumption-loaded, leading, status or shame triggers, and prosecutorial sequences) and five families that move work forward: sensemaking, options and trade-offs, standards and accountability, coaching for growth, and risk and constraints. The move that distinguishes the piece is its insistence that wording and structure, not personality or tone, are usually the bigger lever. It closes with a one-week experiment: write the meeting's intent in five words, bring two matching questions, and note what people volunteered versus withheld. The post carries handbook and subscription promotion, but the argument itself stands on its own.
points: Questions work through three facets, intent, design and signal, and a fuzzy intent makes a question do something else by accident.
Assumption-loaded, leading, shame-trigger and prosecutorial questions all push people to stop solving the problem and start managing their exposure.
Five question families (sensemaking, trade-offs, standards, coaching, risk) each fit a specific moment a manager meets repeatedly.
Resisting the urge to solve problems quickly through coaching questions builds capacity and stops the leader becoming the bottleneck.
A practical test: a good risk question leaves people relieved someone asked it, a poorly pitched one leaves the room tense.
quotes: Questions do a lot more than gather information. They shape the psychological and operational “weather” of a conversation and tell people what matters and whether this is a safe moment to be honest.

When people talk about “bad questions”, they often default to moral framing: good leaders ask good questions and bad leaders ask bad questions. We find it more useful to treat this as a design problem.

The common thread is that all four patterns close down the conversation before it’s had a chance to produce anything useful. The person on the receiving end stops thinking about the problem and starts managing their exposure.
As you grow in seniority, this impulse gets stronger, because pattern recognition speeds up. But solving too quickly limits the other person’s growth and makes you the bottleneck.
The mark of a good risk question is that people feel relieved someone asked it. If your question makes the room tense, revisit your tone. If it makes the room thoughtful, you’ve landed it.
Over time, your questions start doing something understated but decisive: they change what people expect from you. They stop bracing for your summary judgement and start bringing you their thinking.

If you try one thing next week, make it this: pick one meeting, write down the intent in five words, and bring two questions that match it. After the meeting, note what changed: what people volunteered, what they withheld and how quickly you got to a decision.
